boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Marion record (December 17-18, 1864) in Stoneman's Raid into Southwest Virginia [December 1864]: the engagement near Marion between Stoneman's returning column and Breckinridge's force on the 17th and 18th. The fights at Kingsport (13th), Bristol (14th) and Marion and Wytheville against Vaughn (16th), the lead-mine raid and the capture of Saltville (VA082) are context or a separate record. Expedition-wide captures, destruction, prisoners and loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. The frozen side-specific numerical strength bounds are blank (missing_numeric_strength). No figure in this pass is adopted as a simultaneous opening force.

claims.value: The frozen force field reads Divisions for both sides, without bounds; the live field reads zero. Stoneman says Burbridge's force at Cumberland Gap on November 24 was about 4,200 aggregate with four guns by Burbridge's report, and that Gillem put about 1,500 effective men in the field. Breckinridge says that at the close of the 18th he had three brigades and a battalion but fewer than 1,000 men against Stoneman's force of not less than 6,000, and that a body reported as 900 to 1,200 in his rear proved to be some 600.
claims.rationale: A Union force figure from before the march and a Confederate count and estimate at the end of the action; no matched return. None is adopted as a matched opening strength. The live zero is not measured absence.

claims.value: Stoneman says he met Breckinridge in a strong position near Marion, and that Breckinridge escaped by a road over the mountains into North Carolina that was later found blockaded with trees. Breckinridge says he withdrew at 11 p.m. on the 18th by a road south over a mountain range into Rye Valley, difficult for horsemen and thought impracticable for artillery, whose guns were nevertheless got over.
claims.rationale: Ground described by the two commanders; no map verification.

claims.value: Stoneman says no one knew his intentions and the enemy did not learn of the movement until the third day, and that on the 18th Breckinridge, as he afterward learned, found himself nearly surrounded and cut off from Saltville. Breckinridge says intelligence from the front had pointed to a Union withdrawal until the news of December 12, and that after nightfall on the 18th he learned a body of the enemy had passed his right to Seven-Mile Ford.
claims.rationale: Knowledge claimed by each commander; no message log inspected. Stoneman's control of the Bristol telegraph office is context.

claims.value: NPS says the expedition advanced on the lead mines and salt ponds around Marion and Saltville. Stoneman says he had hoped Breckinridge would follow him out of the Saltville fortifications, and sent Gillem around the enemy's left to cut him off from the salt-works. Breckinridge says he followed to join or support Vaughn, judged the lead mines as important as the salt-works, and thought it not creditable to remain at Saltville and surrender the department.
claims.rationale: Stated aims from a summary and the two commanders.

claims.value: The frozen and live commanders are Major Generals George Stoneman and John C. Breckinridge. Stoneman says that on Burbridge's repeated requests for reinforcements he went to the front and assumed immediate control of Burbridge's command for the engagement, and that Wade's and Brown's brigades did all the fighting. Breckinridge says he reinforced Duke with Witcher on his right and withdrew at 11 p.m.; his postscript, answering Burbridge's report, says Stoneman's whole force was present near Marion under Stoneman's command and that the Union force was not met by him while returning but was overtaken while marching up the valley, his report saying Witcher overtook its rear on Saturday between Marion and Mount Airy.
claims.rationale: Command roles from the two commanders; the accounts differ on who met whom, and neither is adopted. The listed commanders do not receive automatic sole credit.

claims.value: The frozen and live results read Union victory; the frozen description says Stoneman defeated a makeshift force on the 17th and destroyed the lead-works and mines on the 18th. Stoneman says Breckinridge, nearly surrounded, withdrew over the mountains in the night of the 18th and that the lead-works were totally destroyed. Breckinridge says Duke and Witcher repulsed the assaults on his right with considerable loss, that he withdrew by the only possible route, and that the damage to the lead mines was reported very slight.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit. The extent of damage at the lead mines is disputed and is campaign context.

claims.value: The frozen casualty field reads 274 total; the live field reads zero. Stoneman says brisk skirmishing through the 18th caused considerable loss in killed and wounded on both sides and that the pursuit next morning took caissons and wagons; his expedition-wide telegram calls the Union loss small and counts 34 officers and 845 enlisted men captured. Breckinridge gives no Marion figure; he says not more than twenty prisoners were taken from his troops, most at Saltville.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. No inspected source gives the frozen 274; the expedition-wide figures are not assigned to this record.

open_questions: Burbridge's No. 2 and Gillem's No. 3 reports, the Confederate reports Nos. 5-16 (Johnston, Witcher, Vaughn, Duke, Echols, Giltner, Cosby, Palmer and others), Steuart's letter on the salt-works damage, returns and maps remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC is one family (the NPS battle pages plus the frozen Arnold rows). George Stoneman's December 27, 1864 telegraphic report and January 6, 1865 report (Official Records Series I, Volume XLV, Part 1, No. 1) are one family of interested Union accounts. John C. Breckinridge's January 3, 1865 report with its postscript (No. 4) is one family of interested Confederate accounts, the same author family as his registered Baton Rouge report and his Bull's Gap reports; its postscript disputes Burbridge's report. The Official Records volume is a shared container, not an additional witness; report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
